name: Nankunshen Daitian Temple
address: No. 976, Kunjiang, Beimen District, Tainan City
description: Almost every Wangye temple in Taiwan with a name people recognize comes back to one place to 'pay respects to the ancestor' — Nankunshen Daitian Temple in Beimen District, Tainan. It is, quite literally, the head temple of Wangye (Royal Lords) worship in Taiwan. This National Monument enshrines the Five Royal Lords — Lords Li, Chi, Wu, Zhu, and Fan — and its standing among Wangye temples could hardly be higher. The temple square is wide open, and the halls are filled with cut-porcelain mosaics, stone carving, and painting. When the pilgrimage season comes around for the Royal Lords' birthdays, processions from branch temples all over Taiwan pour back to the mother temple with drums and gongs roaring — one of the most spectacular religious sights in southern Taiwan.
history: The story begins in 1662, the sixteenth year of the Ming Yongli reign — close to the time Koxinga came to Taiwan — making this one of the oldest Wangye temples on the island. Its most legendary chapter is the 'contest of magic' between the Five Royal Lords and the 'Child Lord' (Gina Gong) of Wanshan Hall. The two sides fought over the same auspicious plot of land, neither able to prevail, until they agreed to share the incense offerings — and to this day the two stand side by side on the site. The temple moved to its present location in 1817, with the new building completed in 1822, and from then on it grew ever grander, hailed as the head temple of Wangye worship. Every year in the late fourth lunar month, during the pilgrimage season, crowds of pilgrims from across Taiwan flood in. It was designated a historic site in 1985 and is today a National Monument.

name: Tainan Grand Mazu Temple
address: No. 18, Ln. 227, Sec. 2, Yongfu Rd, West Central District, Tainan City
description: Tucked into the lanes of Tainan's West Central District, the Tainan Grand Mazu Temple was the first officially built Mazu temple in Taiwan — and before that, it was the palace of the Ming prince Zhu Shugui, the Prince of Ningjing. A Mazu temple converted from a royal residence: you can imagine the stature of the place. After Shi Lang's campaign against Taiwan, the palace became a Tianfei (Heavenly Consort) Temple, and it was later raised to a Tianhou (Empress of Heaven) Temple, becoming the center of Mazu worship in Qing-dynasty Taiwan. Imperial plaques from successive emperors went up one after another, and the temple is rich in historic relics. Anyone hoping for love shouldn't miss Yue Lao, the Old Man Under the Moon, in the rear hall — he is said to help a relationship warm up, and his reputation for answering prayers is known to everyone in Tainan.
history: Around 1684, after Shi Lang's campaign against Taiwan, this palace was turned into a 'Tianfei Temple.' In 1720 it was entered into the official spring and autumn sacrificial rites, and only then renamed the 'Grand Tianhou Temple.' The ground beneath it had once been the residence of Zhu Shugui, the Ming Prince of Ningjing — and in the turn from one dynasty to the next, a prince's palace became a home for Mazu. Thanks to its place in the official rites, the building is laid out with solemn grandeur, and the gold-faced Mazu in the main hall sits dignified and commanding. The temple still holds precious Qing imperial plaques such as 'Glory Over the Seashore' (Huihuang Haishi), and it is listed as a National Monument. As for the Yue Lao in the rear hall, generation after generation of Tainan locals have thought of him first when praying for a partner — making it one of the most popular places in the old capital to ask for love.

name: Tainan Grand Martial Temple
address: No. 229, Sec. 2, Yongfu Rd, West Central District, Tainan City
description: The Tainan Grand Martial Temple (Sidian Wu Temple) is the only temple to Guan Yu in Taiwan entered into the official state rites. It stands in Tainan's West Central District, right beside the Grand Mazu Temple, and its standing is lofty. What no one forgets after a single glance is its rolling red gable wall, a full 66 meters long — a commanding sight and a must-shoot for photographers visiting Tainan. Inside, three halls follow one another in a strict, orderly plan. The main deity is the formidable Guan Sheng Dijun (Guan Gong), his eyes blazing with the bearing of the Martial Saint. Guanyin and Yue Lao are enshrined here as well — and this Yue Lao is the one people come to for severing bad romances and warding off backstabbers, asking him to cut ill-fated ties clean through.
history: In 1665, the nineteenth year of the Ming Yongli reign, Koxinga's son Zheng Jing built this temple, first known as the 'Great Guandi Temple.' It held a place in the state sacrificial rites, and together with the Tainan Confucius Temple it formed a pair: the civil temple and the martial temple. Through repeated renovations and expansions in the Qing dynasty, it took on the three-hall layout seen today, with a mighty, solemn Guan Yu in the main hall. Its most famous treasure is the 'Da Zhang Fu' (A True Man) plaque, presented in 1794 by Yang Tingli, the Taiwan military intendant; among the imperial plaques is 'Wan Shi Ren Ji' (The Pinnacle of Humanity for All Ages) from the Xianfeng era. Together with the far-reaching fame of its Yue Lao, this keeps the incense burning to this day. It is now listed as a National Monument.

name: Fo Guang Shan (Buddha's Light Mountain)
address: No. 153, Xingtian Rd., Dashu Dist., Kaohsiung City
description: From a barren hillside to more than three hundred monasteries and centers around the world — Fo Guang Shan, in Dashu District, Kaohsiung, is one of Taiwan's four great Buddhist mountains and one of its four major Buddhist organizations, founded single-handedly by Master Hsing Yun in 1967. Its best-known landmark is the Buddha Museum: along the Great Path to Buddhahood in front of it, eight pagodas stand in two rows, leading the eye to the great Buddha at the far end — a breathtaking sight. Fo Guang Shan is known for promoting 'Humanistic Buddhism,' the idea that the Dharma does not belong in remote mountains but should be woven into everyone's daily life.
history: In 1949, Master Hsing Yun came to Taiwan with the Nationalist government. In 1967 he bought a stretch of barren hills in Dashu District, Kaohsiung, and began building a monastery — and Fo Guang Shan was born. No one could have imagined that this wild hillside would, over the next fifty-some years, grow into an internationally renowned center of Buddhism. In 2011, the Buddha Museum on the grounds was completed, and it soon became one of southern Taiwan's major religious and tourist destinations.

name: Xingang Fengtian Temple
address: No. 53, Xinmin Rd, Xingang Township, Chiayi County
description: At Xingang Fengtian Temple in Xingang Township, Chiayi County, the Tiger Lord (Huye) doesn't crouch beneath the altar table — he has been invited up onto it, and that is the most distinctive thing about this Mazu temple. Fengtian Temple is known as the temple of the 'Mazu Who Opened Taiwan' (Kaitai Mazu), and it preserves many historic relics and plaques. Since 1988, the Dajia Mazu pilgrimage has made this temple the turning point of its outbound journey, turning it into a sacred destination for worshippers from all over Taiwan.
history: Fengtian Temple traces its origins to a Tianfei temple in Bengang (around present-day Beigang, Yunlin) in 1700. The turning point came in 1799: the Bengang River (today's Beigang River) flooded, washing away the old temple and the settlements around it, and the faithful carried Mazu's golden statue to Mayuanliao (today's Xingang). The new temple was completed in 1811 and named 'Fengtian Temple.' Because of this shared history, Xingang Fengtian Temple and Beigang Chaotian Temple have long disputed which is the true heir of the 'Mazu Who Opened Taiwan.' Generations of rebuilding have left the temple with exquisite cut-porcelain mosaics and koji pottery. Since 1988, the outbound leg of the Dajia Mazu pilgrimage has ended right here at Fengtian Temple, and today it is also a county-designated historic site.

name: Tainan Tiantan (Altar of Heaven)
address: No. 16, Ln. 84, Sec. 2, Zhongyi Rd., West Central Dist., Tainan City
description: Tainan Tiantan, commonly called the 'Tiangong Temple' (Temple of the Lord of Heaven), sits in the heart of Tainan's West Central District. Built jointly by officials and the townspeople, it is dedicated to the supreme Jade Emperor (Yuhuang Dadi). Step into the plain, solemn main hall and look up: a plaque hangs there bearing a single character, 'One' (一). It is one of the 'Three Famous Plaques of the Old Capital' and was designated a general antiquity in 2009. The reasoning is wonderfully clever — the Lord of Heaven is supreme, and however many principles there may be under Heaven, none is greater than the single word 'One.' Every year on the ninth day of the first lunar month, the Jade Emperor's Birthday, worshippers lay out lavish offerings — one of the most solemn days in the old capital's calendar.
history: In 1854, officials, gentry, and merchants of the old capital joined forces to build this altar devoted solely to the Jade Emperor; its site is said to have been an altar for worshipping Heaven back in the Ming Zheng period. The 'One' plaque inside is the temple's best-known feature — its great treasure, and the very thing countless visitors come specially to see. Today it is a municipality-designated historic site.

name: Tainan Confucius Temple
address: No. 2, Nanmen Rd, West Central District, Tainan City
description: Above the East Dacheng Gate hangs a plaque reading 'Quan Tai Shou Xue' — the First School in All Taiwan. The Tainan Confucius Temple was Taiwan's first Confucian temple and the seat of the Taiwan Prefectural School in the Qing dynasty, and those four characters sum up its standing. Set in Tainan's West Central District, it follows the traditional plan of 'school on the left, temple on the right,' with grand and solemn buildings. It is not a Taoist temple, yet it carries great weight in Taiwan's folk belief and cultural heritage. Every year on September 28, Confucius' birthday, the Shidian ceremony is still held according to ancient rites, with young dancers (yisheng) performing the six-row (liuyi) dance — a stop not to be missed for anyone wanting to get close to Chinese culture and Confucian thought.
history: In 1665, the nineteenth year of the Ming Yongli reign, Zheng Jing took the advice of his counselor Chen Yonghua and built this Confucian temple in Taiwan. The aim was simple: to spread learning and cultivate talent in this newly opened land. In the Qing dynasty, the Kangxi Emperor bestowed the plaque 'Wan Shi Shi Biao' (Model Teacher for All Ages), and through many rounds of expansion and repair the temple reached the scale it has today. During the Japanese era it was used as a garrison post and a public school, and in 1945 it was damaged in air raids. Today it is a National Monument and the center of Confucian culture in Taiwan.

name: Chihkan Tower (Fort Provintia)
address: No. 212, Sec. 2, Minzhu Rd, West Central District, Tainan City
description: Chihkan Tower is not a temple — it is one of the best-known historic sites in Tainan's West Central District and a symbol of the city's spirit. It began as Fort Provintia, built by the Dutch, and today's Sea God Temple and Wenchang Pavilion stand tall on the foundations of that old Dutch fort. What makes visitors stop in the garden are the nine bixi — stone tortoise-dragons each bearing a stele — granted by the Qianlong Emperor to commemorate the suppression of the Lin Shuangwen Incident, and heavy with history. And in the Wenchang Pavilion, Kuixing holds his vermilion brush, making this historic site a place where many students also come to pray for success in their exams.
history: In 1653, the Dutch built Fort Provintia here. In 1661, Koxinga captured the fort and established Chengtian Prefecture, and Chihkan changed hands. Over the years that followed, earthquakes and uprisings left most of the fort in ruins; it was not until the Guangxu era of the Qing dynasty that the Sea God Temple, the Wenchang Pavilion, and the Wuzi Shrine were built one by one on the old site. Much of what you see today rests on that rebuilding, with the Dutch fort and the Chinese pavilions layered one over the other — a historic site, rare in Taiwan, where two architectural traditions meet.

name: Donggang Donglong Temple
address: No. 21-1, Donglong St, Donggang Township, Pingtung County
description: Before you even reach Donglong Temple in Donggang Township, Pingtung County, the glittering 'Golden Gateway' in front stops you in your tracks — billed as the largest golden gateway in Taiwan, it blazes in the sunlight. This renowned Wangye temple of southern Taiwan is dedicated to Lord Wen (Wen Fu Qiansui) and is the center of faith for the people of Donggang. What made it famous across the nation is the Donggang Ying Wang Ping'an Festival held every three years — popularly known as the 'burning of the royal boat' — now listed as a nationally important folk cultural asset, vast and mysterious, drawing huge crowds every time. The temple's 'jigai' ritual, in which worshippers receive a symbolic spanking, is also well known; believers trust it to change their luck and drive away misfortune.
history: In 1706, a log inscribed 'Donggang Wen Ji' drifted ashore at Donggang, and the residents built a temple to Lord Wen; only after the tsunami of 1894 was the temple relocated. What all of Taiwan remembers Donglong Temple for is the Donggang Ying Wang Ping'an Festival, held once every three years. The festival lasts eight days, from 'inviting the lords,' when the Royal Lords touring on Heaven's behalf are welcomed ashore, to 'sending off the lords' on the final night, when the ornate royal boat is burned to send them back to the heavenly court — and every step follows strict ancient rites. The royal boat is built by local craftsmen using traditional methods, carved and painted so finely it takes your breath away. On the night of the send-off, crowds of the faithful gather on the shore to watch the flames consume the boat inch by inch — a sight both magnificent and overwhelming. The Donggang Ying Wang festival is now a nationally important folk custom.

name: Chiayi City God Temple
address: No. 168, Wufeng N. Rd, East District, Chiayi City
description: Among all of Taiwan's county-level City God temples, only one has a City God personally ennobled by an emperor: in 1875, the first year of his reign, the Guangxu Emperor conferred on the City God of Chiayi the title 'Marquis Suijing' (Suijing Hou) — a divine rank without equal. This old temple in Chiayi City's East District is thick with incense, and the building you see today was rebuilt in 1940, the fifteenth year of the Showa era. In 2015 it was upgraded to a National Monument, a witness to more than three hundred years of faith in Chiayi. The temple is rich in relics — Qing-dynasty plaques, stone steles, and wood carvings — and the City God's birthday on the second day of the eighth lunar month is one of Chiayi's grandest religious events.
history: This temple's story starts in the winter of 1715, when Zhou Zhongxuan, the magistrate of Zhuluo County, donated his own salary to found this City God temple. In 1764 work began on a rebuilding, finished the following year. Its true moment of glory came in 1875: the Guangxu Emperor ennobled the Chiayi City God as 'Marquis Suijing,' making him the only county-level City God in Taiwan to receive an honorific title from an emperor. The present temple was completed in 1940, the fifteenth year of the Showa era, preserving the building craft of the Japanese period. In 2015 it was upgraded to a National Monument.

name: Fongshan Longshan Temple
address: No. 7, Zhongshan Rd, Fongshan District, Kaohsiung City
description: Fongshan Longshan Temple, in Fengshan District, Kaohsiung, is a Longshan temple from the Qing dynasty and is listed as a National Monument. Like many Longshan temples, it was built by immigrants from the Sanyi area of Quanzhou, with its incense brought over from the Longshan Temple in Jinjiang, Quanzhou. The main deity is Guanyin (Guanshiyin Bodhisattva), and the temple's cut-porcelain mosaics and clay sculptures are especially fine — masterful in technique and well preserved, they are what those in the know come here specifically to see. Amid its simple, solemn atmosphere, this temple, one of the four great old temples of Fengshan, has quietly witnessed the rise and fall of the old town of Fengshan, and it remains an important resource for studying Taiwan's traditional architecture and folk belief.
history: This temple is said to have been founded in the early Qianlong era, though the exact year can no longer be traced. A moving folk story is told about it: early settlers hung the Guanyin incense pouch they carried on a guava tree beside a well, and the pouch glowed in the night. The residents took it as a sign of the bodhisattva's presence, later carved a statue of Guanyin from the tree's branches, and built a temple to enshrine it. By 1764, the temple was already recorded in the 'Revised Gazetteer of Fengshan County' compiled by the magistrate Wang Yingzeng. The buildings you see today mostly reflect repairs made in the Daoguang era and during the Japanese period.

name: Checheng Fu'an Temple
address: No. 51, Fu'an Rd, Checheng Township, Pingtung County
description: Place gold paper at the mouth of the furnace and it is drawn in, sheet after sheet, all on its own — the 'divine cash-counting machine' furnace at Fu'an Temple in Checheng Township, Pingtung County, relies on a precisely designed air convection that leaves worshippers marveling. Checheng Fu'an Temple bills itself as the largest Earth God (Tudi Gong) temple in Taiwan, and its incense burns thick. The main deity, Fude Zhengshen (the Earth God), wears a dragon robe and an official's cap — nothing like the plain Earth God figures seen elsewhere — and legend says this is because he was honored by the Qianlong Emperor. The temple is grand and imposing, and it is the stop most worth making on the drive south toward Kenting.
history: According to the temple, Fu'an Temple was founded in 1662, first called the 'Jingsheng Pavilion,' with Fude Zhengshen as its main deity. In the Jiaqing era it was renamed 'Fu'an Miao' in memory of Fu Kang'an, and in 1951 Chen Cheng gave it the name 'Fu'an Gong.' After Taiwan's retrocession it was expanded several times, its main hall rising lofty and resplendent in gold. Fu'an Temple's best-known tradition is the New Year 'first incense': worshippers once scrambled fiercely to be first during the New Year's Eve countdown, and to prevent crowding and pushing, the temple has since changed it to a 'first incense worship' (bai touxiang). With Kenting National Park right next door, the temple has also become a popular waypoint for travelers heading south to pray for blessings.

name: Pingtung Jiuru Sanshan Guowang Temple
address: No. 174, Ren'ai St., Jiuru Township, Pingtung County
description: Pingtung Jiuru Sanshan Guowang Temple, built in 1778 (the 43rd year of the Qianlong reign), is a Pingtung County historic site dedicated to the three Kings of Jinshan, Mingshan and Dushan. The "Wei Zhen Hai Dong" plaque hanging high in the main hall is dated to the year the temple was built; the worship pavilion is painted with the Hetu and Luoshu diagrams, the door gods are the work of the painter Pan Li-shui, and the wood carvings on the front facade draw on Romance of the Three Kingdoms and Romance of Sui and Tang. Worship here crosses ethnic lines: the temple's most famous legend involves the Hakka of neighboring Linluo, and the Hoklo who later settled in Jiuru carried on the worship.
history: Jiuru Sanshan Guowang Temple was completed in 1778 (the 43rd year of the Qianlong reign), and the "Wei Zhen Hai Dong" plaque in the main hall dates from that year. In 1866 (the 5th year of the Tongzhi reign), the temple was rebuilt on its present site; it was renovated again in the late 1920s, and its most recent restoration was completed in October 2016. In front of the temple stands a bluestone incense burner from 1807 (the 12th year of the Jiaqing reign). In 2004, the Pingtung County Government designated it a county historic site, and in 2012 its left and right side wings were separately registered as historic buildings.

name: Xinying Taizi Temple
address: No. 45-2, Taizigong, Taibei Vil., Xinying District, Tainan City
description: Xinying Taizi Temple is regarded as the founding mother temple of Marshal Zhongtan — the Third Prince, Nezha — with branch temples spread far and wide that return each year to pay respects to their ancestor. The grandest day comes in the ninth lunar month: around the Third Prince's birthday, sedan chairs from branch temples everywhere arrive one after another to gather incense in Xinying, and the roads overflow with procession troupes. The temple grounds hold two temples, old and new. The old temple is listed as a Tainan City historic site — small in scale, but it is where the roots lie — while the new temple takes in the pilgrim crowds from all over. To see Third Prince worship in its most original form, step into the old temple first: that is where all this celebration began.
history: In 1663, the second year of the Kangxi reign, five believers — Xu Peiyuan, Hong Jizhou, He Shiping, Zhou Yide, and Li Zhongcheng — fled the turmoil of war, bringing their families and the golden statue and sedan chair of Marshal Zhongtan across the sea to Taiwan, landing at Yichagang. After they settled in the Xinying area, the faith gradually took root in the villages, and in 1688 the Taizi Temple was built, regarded as the founding mother temple of Taiwan's Third Prince temples. Over more than three hundred years, branch temples have spread across Taiwan, and every year on the ninth day of the ninth lunar month, the Third Prince's birthday, the deities of the branch temples return here to gather incense — one temple's birthday has become a shared homecoming for Third Prince worship across Taiwan. The old temple building still stands today and is listed as a Tainan City historic site.

name: Chukou Longyin Temple
address: No. 1, Chukou Village, Fanlu Township, Chiayi County
description: Ji Gong, with his tattered hat, tattered fan and ragged robe, was once filmed at this very temple. According to the temple, both TTV's drama series Ji Gong and CTV's drama series Ji Gong the Living Buddha chose Chukou Longyin Temple in Fanlu, Chiayi, as a filming location. Longyin Temple is dedicated to Chan Master Ji Gong, the much-loved Living Buddha Ji Gong. It sits at the foot of Chukou Mountain on the way toward Alishan, within the Alishan National Scenic Area. The large stone panels on either side of the main entrance are carved with scenes of Ji Gong guiding people toward salvation, and the eaves are covered with auspicious dragons in cut-porcelain mosaic. The Yuantong Hall on the second floor enshrines Guanyin Bodhisattva, flanked by Manjushri and Samantabhadra. The temple has set lunar 10/3 as the day Chan Master Ji Gong attained the Way, and each year a birthday ceremony is held that morning during the chen hour. It is the liveliest day of the year.
history: According to the temple's history, from 1966 onward a local family named Qiu repeatedly dreamed of a deity in ragged clothes holding a tattered fan, who told them to carve a statue. In 1974 the Qiu family brought a divided spirit of Chan Master Ji Gong from Longfeng Temple in Jiaxian, Kaohsiung. That same year the statue was carved and enshrined in their home, and they began consulting the deity on behalf of devotees and helping people. In August 1990, construction of Longyin Temple began with almost no funds. At first it relied on devotees working as volunteers; only later was a management committee gradually formed. On October 24, 1991, the structure of the inner hall was largely complete, and Chan Master Ji Gong was installed there ahead of the rest. According to the temple, TTV's Ji Gong was filmed here in August 1995 and CTV's Ji Gong the Living Buddha in June 1997, and so this new temple at the foot of the mountain came to be seen on television by many people.

visit.gettingThere: The temple lists two public transit routes: take the Taiwan Tourist Shuttle from THSR Chiayi Station, or take a Chiayi Bus from the main station in downtown Chiayi, and get off at Chukou stop either way. Some Chiayi Bus services do not run on weekends and holidays, so check the latest timetable before you set out.
visit.whenToGo: Lunar 10/3 is the day the temple has set for Chan Master Ji Gong's attainment of the Way, and a birthday ceremony is held that day during the chen hour (7–9 AM). According to the temple, a fire-walking ceremony is usually held on the festival day, and it draws the biggest crowds.

name: Guanziling Huowangye Temple
address: No. 24-38, Guanling Village, Baihe District, Tainan City
description: On the opening night of the autumn Guanziling Hot Spring Food Festival, an illuminated Acala float sets out from the Baoquan Bridge parking lot and is pulled up the mountain road to Dacheng Hall Plaza, with people in yukata carrying lanterns in the procession. The deity being carried out is the main god of Guanziling Huowangye Temple. Huowangye, the Fire King, is Acala (Fudo Myoo). In the early years of Japanese rule, when the hot springs were being developed, the Japanese set up an image of Acala above the spring source to pray for safety. Later the statue and its stone tablet were taken away, so local residents pooled money to build a temple, recreated the statue after the original, and gave it a name that came more naturally to Taiwanese tongues. The temple is small, yet it is the center of faith for Guanziling's hot spring businesses and residents. Each year the hot spring operators choose an incense master (luzhu) by divination to lead the offerings, praying that the springs never run dry. Before you soak, stop by to meet the guardian of these mud hot springs.
history: In 1902, the Japanese developed the Guanziling hot springs and set up an image of Acala above the spring source to pray for safety. Later the Japanese took the statue and stone tablet away, and local people pooled money to build this temple, modeling a new statue on the original Acala. From then on he was called Huowangye, the Fire King. Each year the hot spring operators choose an incense master (luzhu) by divination to lead the offerings, praying that the springs keep flowing, and he became the guardian of the Guanziling hot springs. In recent years, events held by the Tainan City Government and the Siraya National Scenic Area Administration have referred to him as "Acala (Huowangye)." In the summer of 2022, the Siraya National Scenic Area Administration held a float festival timed to Huowangye's birthday, and in the summer of 2026 it held an Acala-themed street parade. The Tainan City Government Tourism Bureau, for its part, schedules the Acala night procession for the opening of the hot spring food festival each year. The wisdom king the Japanese brought here a century ago now walks the hot spring streets with the residents every year.

visit.whenToGo: On the opening night of the autumn Guanziling Hot Spring Food Festival, an Acala night procession runs from around the Baoquan Bridge parking lot to Dacheng Hall Plaza. The date changes from year to year (September 17, 2022; September 21, 2024; October 25, 2025), so check the Tainan City Government Tourism Bureau's announcements before you go. In summer, the Siraya National Scenic Area Administration has also held a float festival and a street parade timed to Huowangye's birthday.
